cv-joint-click-corolla.licence_note: Manufacturer service bulletin (copyright Toyota Motor Sales USA) on NHTSA's public bulletin archive. Only the technical fact is used, restated in our own words; no text or images copied.

cv-joint-click-outer.fact: BMW service information SI B31 01 17, for the X5 M (F85) and X6 M (F86) only, traces a hard clacking from the front axle, heard when turning and pulling away from a stop under moderate to heavy acceleration, to premature wear of the outer (wheel-side) CV joints.
cv-joint-click-outer.licence_note: Manufacturer service bulletin (copyright BMW of North America) on NHTSA's public bulletin archive. Only the technical fact is used, restated in our own words; no text or images copied.

cv-joint-fwd-role.fact: CV joints are commonly used in front-wheel-drive cars to deliver engine power to the front wheels while still letting them steer.
cv-joint-fwd-role.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

riding-the-clutch.fact: Riding the clutch means needlessly keeping the clutch partly disengaged (the pedal not fully let up): the disc then slips against the flywheel, and the disc and flywheel wear early. Merely resting a foot on the pedal is usually too light to slip the disc, but it keeps the release bearing pressed and spinning, and the bearing fails early.
riding-the-clutch.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

clutch-hill-hold.fact: Holding the car on a hill with the clutch makes it slip, which wears it much like a brake pad wears when stopping.
clutch-hill-hold.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

cvt-how-it-works.fact: A belt CVT runs a belt between two pulleys whose halves move apart or together to change their effective diameter, which lets the engine hold a steady speed while the car accelerates.
cvt-how-it-works.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

flood-car-signs.fact: Signs of a flood-damaged car: mud or sand under the seats or dashboard, rust around the doors, loose, stained or mismatched carpet, and a smell of mould or decay, or a strong cleaning-product smell covering it.
flood-car-signs.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

flood-damage-slow.fact: Water damage can slowly destroy a car's mechanical and electrical systems and cause rust and corrosion, so a mechanic should inspect a suspected flood car.
flood-damage-slow.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

flood-database-gaps.fact: The NICB's free US database shows whether a car was flood-damaged, stolen or declared salvage, but only if it was insured when the damage happened.
flood-database-gaps.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

lpg-propane-butane-mix.fact: LPG is a mix of propane and butane; in northern-hemisphere winters the mix contains more propane, in summer more butane.
lpg-propane-butane-mix.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

lpg-heavier-than-air.fact: LPG gas is heavier than air: it flows along floors and settles in low spots such as basements, unlike natural gas.
lpg-heavier-than-air.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

lpg-smell-added.fact: A powerful odorant (ethanethiol) is added to LPG so that leaks can be detected easily.
lpg-smell-added.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

lpg-tank-80-percent.fact: LPG tanks are typically filled to only 80-85% of capacity, leaving room for the liquid to expand as it warms (Liquefied petroleum gas); modern autogas fill valves usually have an automatic fill limiter that prevents overfilling (Autogas).
lpg-tank-80-percent.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

lpg-reducer-coolant.fact: In an autogas system the converter (vaporiser/reducer) turns liquid LPG into vapour; evaporating LPG absorbs heat, so engine coolant is circulated through the converter to warm it.
lpg-reducer-coolant.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

propane-octane.fact: Propane has a higher octane rating than gasoline: 104-112, compared with 87-92 for US gasoline (US AKI scale).
propane-octane.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

propane-less-energy.fact: A gallon of propane holds about 27% less energy than a gallon of gasoline, so propane vehicles cover fewer kilometres per litre.
propane-less-energy.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

cng-pressure.fact: CNG (mostly methane) is stored in high-pressure tanks at about 200-250 bar.
cng-pressure.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

cng-lighter-than-air.fact: Natural gas is lighter than air, so it disperses more readily when released, whereas LPG settles in low places.
cng-lighter-than-air.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

cng-tank-expiry.fact: US guidance (AFDC): CNG tanks have a useful life of 15 to 20 years; every tank carries a 'DO NOT USE AFTER' date label, and an expired tank must be replaced and made unusable.
cng-tank-expiry.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

cng-tank-inspection.fact: US guidance: light-duty CNG tanks should be inspected every 3 years or 36,000 miles (about 58,000 km), whichever comes first, and after any fire, accident or other incident that could damage them.
cng-tank-inspection.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

vin-17-characters.fact: A modern VIN has 17 characters, and the letters I, O and Q are never used in it so they cannot be confused with 1 and 0. The US made the 17-character format mandatory in 1981.
vin-17-characters.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

vin-check-digit.fact: On VINs for North America and China the 9th character is a check digit calculated from the other characters, so one mistyped character usually breaks it. A match is not proof the VIN is right: there is about a 1 in 11 chance that a wrong VIN still matches. In Europe the check digit is not compulsory.
vin-check-digit.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

vin-model-year.fact: On North American VINs the 10th character is the model year: 2001 to 2009 are the digits 1 to 9, and 2010 starts again at A, so J is 2018 and K is 2019. Letters repeat every 30 years; on cars a digit in the 7th position means 1980 to 2009 and a letter means 2010 to 2039. Outside North America the 10th character is usually 0.
vin-model-year.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

vin-wmi-country.fact: The first three VIN characters (the WMI) identify the maker, and the first one usually shows the country of manufacture: J is Japan, W Germany, KL to KR South Korea, and 1, 4 and 5 the United States. A Honda whose VIN starts with 1HG was built by Honda in Ohio.
vin-wmi-country.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

obd-socket-location.fact: OBD-II cars have a standard diagnostic socket that must be within 0.61 m (2 feet) of the steering wheel. OBD-II became mandatory for US passenger cars from model year 1996; the European version (EOBD) for petrol cars from 2001 and for diesel cars from 2004.
obd-socket-location.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

catalyst-precious-metals.fact: A three-way catalytic converter turns carbon monoxide, unburnt fuel and nitrogen oxides in the exhaust into less harmful gases. It works with platinum-group metals (platinum, palladium and rhodium), which is why catalytic converters are a target for thieves.
catalyst-precious-metals.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

turbo-driven-by-exhaust.fact: A turbocharger is powered by the engine's own exhaust: the exhaust spins a turbine, which turns a compressor that pushes extra air into the engine. A supercharger does the same job but is driven mechanically, usually by a belt from the crankshaft.
turbo-driven-by-exhaust.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

differential-why.fact: In a turn the outer wheels travel farther than the inner ones, so they must turn faster. A differential lets the two wheels on a driven axle rotate at different speeds; vehicles without one, like go-karts, rely on the tyres slipping in corners.
differential-why.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

diesel-no-spark-plugs.fact: A diesel engine has no spark plugs: it compresses air until it is hot enough to ignite the fuel as it is injected (compression ignition). Some diesels, especially indirect-injection types, are harder to start and need glow plugs.
diesel-no-spark-plugs.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

dpf-needs-a-drive.fact: A diesel particulate filter traps soot and must burn it off from time to time (regeneration). This needs higher road speeds than city streets usually allow, so a diesel driven only in town traffic may need regular faster drives; ignoring the warning light too long can ruin the filter so it must be replaced.
dpf-needs-a-drive.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

immobiliser-chip-key.fact: An immobiliser lets the engine start only when it recognises the electronic chip (transponder) in the correct key. Immobilisers have been mandatory on all new cars in Germany since 1 January 1998 and in the UK since 1 October 1998.
immobiliser-chip-key.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

speedometer-reads-high.fact: Under UN regulation ECE R39 a speedometer may never show less than the true speed, and may show at most 10% plus 4 km/h more at the test speeds. Tyre size affects the reading too: most speedometers have tolerances of about plus or minus 10%, mainly because of differences in tyre diameter.
speedometer-reads-high.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

fuel-filler-arrow.fact: On many dashboards a small arrow next to the fuel-pump icon points to the side of the car where the fuel filler is. The icon-and-arrow idea came from Ford designer Jim Moylan in 1986.
fuel-filler-arrow.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

headlamp-lens-cloudy.fact: Plastic (polycarbonate) headlamp lenses turn cloudy and yellow because ultraviolet light from the sun and the bulbs oxidises the lens hardcoat. Mild haze can be polished out, but sanding without a new UV-resistant clear coat makes the lens degrade faster. Aim matters too: misaimed headlamps are dangerous and ineffective.
headlamp-lens-cloudy.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

snow-chains-slow.fact: Snow chains go on the driven wheels and are for slow driving: chain manuals generally set a maximum of about 30 to 50 km/h.
snow-chains-slow.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

esc-mandatory-dates.fact: Electronic stability control brakes individual wheels to keep the car going where the steering points. It became mandatory on new passenger cars in the US from model year 2012 and on all newly registered cars in the EU from 1 November 2014; in Europe it had saved an estimated 15,000 lives by 2020.
esc-mandatory-dates.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

airbag-milliseconds.fact: In a frontal crash the decision to fire the airbags is typically made within 15 to 30 milliseconds, and the front airbags are fully inflated within about 60 to 80 milliseconds. Airbags are a supplemental restraint system (SRS), designed to work with the seat belt, not to replace it.
airbag-milliseconds.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

rear-facing-seat-airbag.fact: A rear-facing infant seat in a front seat with an active airbag puts the baby's head close to the airbag, and its deployment can cause severe head injuries or death. Some cars have a switch to disable the front passenger airbag.
rear-facing-seat-airbag.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

hot-car-window-myth.fact: At 21 °C outside, a car standing in direct sun can pass 49 °C inside within a short time; children and older people can suffer heat stroke in minutes, and a window left slightly open does not prevent it.
hot-car-window-myth.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

who-seatbelt-child-restraint.fact: WHO: wearing a seat belt cuts the risk of death for people in a vehicle by as much as 50%, and using child restraints can cut deaths of infants by 71%.
who-seatbelt-child-restraint.licence_note: World Health Organization fact sheet (copyright WHO). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

who-speed-risk.fact: WHO: each 1% rise in average speed raises the risk of a fatal crash by 4% and the risk of a serious crash by 3%. For a pedestrian struck by the front of a car, the risk of dying is 4.5 times higher at 65 km/h than at 50 km/h.
who-speed-risk.licence_note: World Health Organization fact sheet (copyright WHO). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

who-phone-hands-free.fact: WHO: a driver on a mobile phone is roughly 4 times as likely to crash; hands-free use is not much safer than holding the phone, and texting raises the risk a lot.
who-phone-hands-free.licence_note: World Health Organization fact sheet (copyright WHO). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

who-road-deaths-young.fact: WHO: road crashes kill about 1.16 million people a year, and for people aged 5 to 29 (children and young adults) road injuries are the top cause of death.
who-road-deaths-young.licence_note: World Health Organization fact sheet (copyright WHO). Only the facts and figures are used, restated in our own words, no text copied.

benz-patent-1886.fact: Carl Benz filed his patent application for a motor carriage on 29 January 1886; the patent, DRP 37435, gave the Benz Patent-Motorwagen its name.
benz-patent-1886.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

bertha-benz-first-trip.fact: On 5 August 1888 Bertha Benz made the first long-distance drive in a petrol car, about 106 km from Mannheim to Pforzheim in the Patent-Motorwagen. Its fuel, a solvent called ligroin, was sold only by pharmacies, so the pharmacy in Wiesloch became the world's first filling station.
bertha-benz-first-trip.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

bertha-benz-brake-lining.fact: On that same 1888 trip Bertha Benz used her hat pin to clear a blocked fuel line, and when the wooden brakes started to give out she had a shoemaker cover them with leather: the first brake linings.
bertha-benz-brake-lining.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

model-t-assembly-line.fact: Ford's moving assembly line started on 7 October 1913 and cut the time to build a Model T from about 12.5 hours to 93 minutes by 1914. More than 15 million Model Ts were sold.
model-t-assembly-line.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

model-t-any-colour-black.fact: Henry Ford later wrote that in 1909 he told his managers customers could have a car in any colour as long as it was black; the black-only policy was actually put into practice only in 1914.
model-t-any-colour-black.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

wiper-mary-anderson.fact: Mary Anderson was granted a patent for a hand-operated windshield wiper in 1903. Potential buyers saw no commercial value in it, and her 17-year patent expired in 1920 without the device going into mass production.
wiper-mary-anderson.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

electric-starter-1912.fact: Before the electric starter, cars were started with a hand crank. Charles Kettering's electrical system for starting, ignition and lighting went into Cadillac's 1912 models, for which Cadillac ordered 12,000 self-starters.
electric-starter-1912.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

first-traffic-light-1868.fact: In December 1868, before any car existed, the first traffic signals went up outside London's Houses of Parliament, so that fewer police officers were needed to direct traffic. A policeman moved semaphore arms by day and worked red and green lamps at night; on 2 January 1869 the signal exploded and was removed.
first-traffic-light-1868.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

three-point-belt-free-patent.fact: The modern three-point seat belt was developed by Nils Bohlin for Volvo, which introduced it as standard in 1959, and Volvo then made the patent open so other car makers could use the design for free. Bohlin showed its effect in a study of 28,000 crashes in Sweden.
three-point-belt-free-patent.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

abs-first-1978.fact: One of the first electronic four-wheel anti-lock braking systems, made by Bosch, was offered as an option on the Mercedes-Benz S-Class (W116) from 1978.
abs-first-1978.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

first-speeding-fine-1896.fact: Walter Arnold of East Peckham in Kent is thought to be the first driver ever convicted of speeding: on 28 January 1896 he went at 8 mph (13 km/h) and was fined 1 shilling plus costs. Under the 1865 Red Flag Act the town limit was 2 mph (3 km/h).
first-speeding-fine-1896.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

cruise-control-blind-inventor.fact: Cruise control was invented by Ralph Teetor, who was blind. Family lore says that riding with his lawyer, who slowed down while talking and sped up while listening, annoyed him into inventing a speed control; his 'Speedostat' was patented in 1950, and Cadillac marketed it as 'Cruise Control'.
cruise-control-blind-inventor.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

rear-view-mirror-1911.fact: The earliest known rear-view mirror on a racing car was on Ray Harroun's Marmon at the first Indianapolis 500 in 1911; Harroun said the rough brick track shook it so much that it was of little use. Mirrors for cars had already been written about in 1906, and an adjustable dashboard mirror was sold in 1908.
rear-view-mirror-1911.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

crumple-zone-patent.fact: Mercedes-Benz patent No. 854157, granted in 1952 to engineer Béla Barényi's design, divided the car body into a rigid passenger compartment and front and rear crumple zones that absorb crash energy, against the old belief that a safe car had to be rigid. The first Mercedes body built with it was the 1959 W111.
crumple-zone-patent.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

leaded-petrol-end-2021.fact: Leaded petrol for cars was phased out worldwide only in July 2021, when Algeria stopped selling it; the UN Environment Programme declared its official end on 30 August 2021. Lead poisons catalytic converters, so cars with one can run only on unleaded fuel.
leaded-petrol-end-2021.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

prius-first-hybrid.fact: The Toyota Prius was the first mass-produced hybrid car: it went on sale in Japan in 1997 and worldwide in 2000.
prius-first-hybrid.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

corolla-best-seller.fact: The Toyota Corolla has been the best-selling car nameplate of all time since 1997, when it passed the Volkswagen Beetle; Toyota reached 50 million Corollas sold in 2021.
corolla-best-seller.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

beetle-last-one-2003.fact: The original Volkswagen Beetle was built from 1938 to 2003; the last one left the Puebla plant in Mexico on 30 July 2003, after 21,529,464 had been made, the most of any car on a single platform.
beetle-last-one-2003.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

jdm-180-limit.fact: Most cars built for Japan's home market are limited to 180 km/h. The limit is self-imposed by the makers through the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association and is not a legal requirement.
jdm-180-limit.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

kei-car-rules.fact: Japan's kei cars are limited by law to 3.4 m long, 1.48 m wide, under 2.0 m high and an engine under 660 cc; a gentlemen's agreement among makers also caps power at 64 PS.
kei-car-rules.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

japan-shaken-inspection.fact: Under Japan's shaken programme a private car needs its first inspection after three years and then one every two years.
japan-shaken-inspection.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

fuel-saving-gadgets-myth.fact: The US EPA tested over 100 supposed fuel-saving devices, such as fuel-line magnets and mixture 'enhancers'; very few gave any benefit, and some could damage the engine or increase exhaust emissions.
fuel-saving-gadgets-myth.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

phone-at-pump-myth.fact: The story that a mobile phone can ignite petrol at a pump has not been reproduced under any controlled conditions; phone makers and stations still ask people to switch phones off. The documented refuelling fires involve static electricity: a driver who does not first touch a conductive part of the car carries the charge to the nozzle, and many stations warn against leaving the pump while refuelling.
phone-at-pump-myth.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

petrol-in-diesel-damage.fact: Petrol in a diesel is the costly mix-up: in a modern diesel even one litre of petrol can wreck the injection pump for good, because petrol does not lubricate it. Diesel put in a petrol engine makes heavy smoke but, drained as soon as it is noticed, usually leaves no lasting damage.
petrol-in-diesel-damage.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

aggressive-driving-fuel.fact: Aggressive driving (speeding, rapid acceleration and hard braking) can lower fuel economy by roughly 15% to 30% at highway speeds and 10% to 40% in stop-and-go traffic.
aggressive-driving-fuel.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

speed-above-80-fuel.fact: Every car has its own most efficient speed, but fuel economy usually drops rapidly above about 80 km/h (50 mph).
speed-above-80-fuel.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

extra-weight-fuel.fact: An extra 100 pounds (about 45 kg) in the car can reduce fuel economy by about 1%; the effect is larger on smaller cars.
extra-weight-fuel.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

roof-box-fuel.fact: A large, blunt roof-top cargo box can reduce fuel economy by around 2% to 8% in city driving, 6% to 17% on the highway and 10% to 25% at 105 to 120 km/h (65 to 75 mph).
roof-box-fuel.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

cruise-control-saves-fuel.fact: On the highway, cruise control helps hold a constant speed and in most cases saves fuel.
cruise-control-saves-fuel.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). Restated in our own words.

odometer-rollback-scale.fact: A 2002 NHTSA study estimated that 450,000 vehicles a year were sold in the US with false odometer readings, costing buyers over $1 billion a year. Digital odometers can be even easier to tamper with, often through the OBD2 port; wear on floor mats and pedal rubber that does not fit the mileage is a warning sign.
odometer-rollback-scale.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

salvage-title-meaning.fact: In the US a 'salvage' title brand goes on a car that an insurer paid out on as damaged or a total loss; how much damage that takes depends on the state, from 50% to 95% of the car's value. 'Salvage', 'rebuilt' and similar brands differ from state to state, and a car exported from the US can get a clean title whatever its history.
salvage-title-meaning.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

title-washing.fact: 'Title washing' means re-registering a car in another jurisdiction for the purpose of removing a brand such as 'salvage' from its title; vehicle history reports are meant to reveal it.
title-washing.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

recall-check-by-vin.fact: Any US car's 17-character VIN can be checked free on NHTSA's recall site for unrepaired safety recalls; the search does not show recalls more than 15 years old, unless a maker offers longer coverage.
recall-check-by-vin.licence_note: US federal government work, public domain (17 U.S.C. 105). nhtsa.gov blocks automated fetching, so the fact was checked through the site's own indexed page text; restated in our own words.

takata-airbag-recall.fact: The Takata airbag recall is the largest car recall in US history, covering more than 42 million US cars; by January 2024 over 100 million inflators had been recalled worldwide by more than 20 car makers. A faulty inflator can rupture and throw metal fragments, and Takata said the issue was linked to hot, humid locations.
takata-airbag-recall.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

us-used-cars-to-georgia.fact: Georgia is one of the main destinations for used American-made vehicles: an October 2020 report put the United Arab Emirates first, followed by Nigeria and Georgia.
us-used-cars-to-georgia.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

miles-to-km.fact: American odometers count miles: one international mile is exactly 1.609344 km, so 100,000 miles is about 160,934 km.
miles-to-km.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

georgia-car-trade-2025.fact: Geostat data for 2025: motor cars were Georgia's top export, USD 2.8 billion or 38.6% of all exports, and motor vehicles were also the top import, USD 3.8 billion or 20.9% of imports.
georgia-car-trade-2025.licence_note: News report (facts only, restated in our own words, no text copied). Secondary source: prefer the official act if the figure is ever disputed.

ge-inspection-schedule.fact: Georgia's periodic technical inspection started on 1 January 2018 and has been mandatory for every vehicle category since 1 January 2019. A passenger car (category M1) is inspected every second year once it is 4 years old, and every year once it is 8 years old.
ge-inspection-schedule.licence_note: Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development of Georgia, official page. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words.

ge-inspection-checklist.fact: Georgia's periodic inspection checks the vehicle's identification, braking system, steering, visibility, lamps, reflectors and electrics, axles, wheels, tyres and suspension, the chassis, and environmental nuisance such as exhaust emissions.
ge-inspection-checklist.licence_note: Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development of Georgia, official page. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words.

ge-steering-conversion-fails.fact: Georgia (the economy ministry's inspection page, rules from 2018, under right-hand-drive vehicles): a right-hand-drive car first registered in Georgia after 1 January 2018 cannot pass the periodic inspection if its steering system has been further changed, and once an inspection from that date has recorded the steering wheel's side, moving the wheel again also means the car cannot pass.
ge-steering-conversion-fails.licence_note: Ministry of Economy and Sustainable Development of Georgia, official page. Only the facts are used, restated in our own words.

ge-gas-sticker.fact: Georgia (Government Resolution No. 80 of 15 January 2014, for equipment that runs a car on natural gas, i.e. methane/CNG): this gas-cylinder equipment gets its own compliance check, and a car that passes gets a round blue sticker 90 mm across in the lower right corner of the windshield, with its expiry month in red figures. The resolution's forms call it a mandatory yearly assessment.
ge-gas-sticker.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-gas-no-fill-overdue.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 80, natural gas / CNG): a driver must not fill gas cylinders that have not passed their next periodic check and lack the matching stamp, and must not fill them if a leak has been found in the gas lines or joints.
ge-gas-no-fill-overdue.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-gas-smell-stop.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 80, natural gas / CNG): if the driver smells gas while driving, they must stop at once, fix the fault if they can or close the supply valve, and go to a gas-equipment service.
ge-gas-smell-stop.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-gas-extinguisher-no-flame.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 80, natural gas / CNG): every vehicle with natural-gas cylinders must carry a fire extinguisher and a felt fire blanket, and in cold weather the engine and frozen gas lines may be warmed only with hot water, hot air or steam, never an open flame.
ge-gas-extinguisher-no-flame.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-gas-cylinder-rejected.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 80, natural gas / CNG): a cylinder is refused at the check if it lacks the required markings (maker's mark, number, dates of manufacture and periodic check, working and test pressure, mass) or some of them cannot be read, or if it has cracks, damaged threads, or gouges and scratches deeper than 10% of the wall thickness.
ge-gas-cylinder-rejected.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-gas-filling-order.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 80): at the station, natural gas cylinders are filled with the engine off and the outlet valve closed, up to the working pressure of 20 MPa (200 atm); afterwards the outlet valve is opened gradually, and only then is the engine started.
ge-gas-filling-order.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-speed-limits.fact: Georgian traffic law for category B cars: up to 60 km/h in built-up areas and 20 km/h in residential zones; elsewhere up to 110 km/h on motorways and 90 km/h on other roads, or 80 km/h on any road when towing a light trailer. Road signs can set different limits.
ge-speed-limits.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-children-front-seat.fact: Georgian traffic law: children under 12 may not ride in a car's front seat. A child under 3 in the back must sit in a child seat or restraint that fits their height and weight, or on the lap of a back-seat passenger aged at least 16 who wears a seat belt, with no more than one child per lap.
ge-children-front-seat.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-seatbelt-who-must.fact: Georgian traffic law: the driver must wear a seat belt and make sure the passenger beside them wears one, as must a rear passenger aged 16 or over who holds a child under 3 on their lap.
ge-seatbelt-who-must.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-phone-ban.fact: Georgian traffic law: drivers may not use a mobile phone while driving, except through a headset or a loudspeaker (remote) talk function while both hands stay free for driving.
ge-phone-ban.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-dazzled-stop-hazards.fact: Georgian traffic law: if oncoming headlights dazzle you, slow down without changing lanes, stop and switch on the hazard lights; drive on only once your sight has fully recovered.
ge-dazzled-stop-hazards.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-tunnel-rules.fact: Georgian traffic law: in a tunnel marked by a road sign, the headlights (dipped or main beam) must be on even if the tunnel is lit; reversing and U-turns are banned, and stopping is allowed only in an emergency, in a marked bay if there is one.
ge-tunnel-rules.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-fog-lamp-colours.fact: Georgian traffic law: front fog lamps, if fitted, must give white or selective yellow light, two on a car, and no part of their lit surface may be above the top of the dipped headlamps; rear fog lamps must be red.
ge-fog-lamp-colours.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-winter-tyre-period.fact: Georgia (Government Resolution No. 526, in force since 1 January 2024): from 1 December to 1 March, every wheel must have proper winter tyres on the road sections the resolution lists; in extreme weather the Interior Minister can set a different period.
ge-winter-tyre-period.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-winter-tyre-spec.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 526): a tyre counts as a winter tyre only if less than 10 years have passed since its manufacture date, the date is readable, the tread is at least 3 mm deep on cars (4 mm on buses) and it carries the snowflake symbol.
ge-winter-tyre-spec.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-winter-roads-list.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 526) lists the winter-tyre road sections, among them Mleta to Kobi on the Gudauri road, the Rikoti tunnel to Tseva, Borjomi to Bakuriani and Akhalkalaki, Jvari to Mestia and Lasdili, and Tbilisi to Tianeti.
ge-winter-roads-list.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-winter-chains-police.fact: Georgia (Resolution No. 526): in extreme weather the police can also require anti-skid chains on all wheels of at least one driven axle; chains must be factory-made, fit the tyre size and be used only on snow or ice, and a driver without proper tyres or chains can be refused entry to the section.
ge-winter-chains-police.licence_note: Official legal act of Georgia on matsne.gov.ge (the Legislative Herald). Official texts of laws and decrees are not protected by copyright under Georgian copyright law; restated in our own words.

ge-jvari-pass-bypass.fact: The Jvari Pass, at 2,379 m, is the highest point of the road from Tbilisi to the Russian border; in about 25 km the road climbs more than 1,000 m to reach it. Because the pass is prone to heavy snowfall, a 23 km bypass from Kvesheti to Kobi with a 9 km tunnel, the longest in the region, has been under construction since 2021.
ge-jvari-pass-bypass.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

ge-rikoti-tunnel.fact: The Rikoti Pass (996 m) divides Georgia into its western and eastern parts; the Tbilisi to Kutaisi highway passes through it in a 1,722 m rock-cut tunnel built in 1982.
ge-rikoti-tunnel.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

ge-number-plates.fact: Georgia's current number plates, two letters, three digits and two letters (AA-123-AA), have been issued since 1 September 2014, with the flag and 'GE' on a blue strip; the country code changed from GEO to GE in 2010.
ge-number-plates.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.

ge-old-plate-regions.fact: On Georgian plates of the 1993 to 2014 format, the first letter originally showed where the car was registered: A Tbilisi, B Adjara, D Kutaisi, E Rustavi, O Gori, R Telavi and so on, until the system ran out in 2004.
ge-old-plate-regions.licence_note: Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the fact is used, restated in our own words, no text copied (facts are not copyrightable); credit Wikipedia if ever quoted.
